security_spec.violation_condition: Linux kernel in S-mode accesses stopei, eip[k], or eie[k] CSRs while mstateen0 bit 58 (IMSIC state enable) is zero, either because M-mode firmware (e.g., OpenSBI) did not set it, or because the kernel failed to check the bit before touching these CSRs even though the Smstateen extension is implemented in hardware.
security_spec.summary: Access to ACLIC-reused IMSIC CSRs (stopei, eip, eie) from S-mode is now gated by mstateen0 bit 58; if M-mode firmware or early kernel init neglects to check/set this bit, any AIA interrupt delivery path will trap with an illegal instruction exception, crashing the kernel.

findings.finding: S-mode csr_swap(CSR_TOPEI, 0) accesses STOPEI (0x15c) on the critical external-interrupt hot path without any prior check that mstateen0 bit 58 (IMSIC state enable) is set. If M-mode firmware left mstateen0[58]=0, every external interrupt delivery via IMSIC causes an illegal-instruction trap and the kernel cannot handle any IMSIC-delivered interrupts. The kernel cannot even read mstateen0 from S-mode — it must trust M-mode firmware, but no runtime validation of sstateen0[58] exists either.

imsic_csr_read() writes CSR_SISELECT (0x150) then reads CSR_SIREG (0x151) to access IMSIC EIP[k]/EIE[k] registers indirectly. Under Smstateen, accessing these registers via ISELECT/IREG when mstateen0[58]=0 causes an illegal-instruction exception. No gating check on mstateen0 or sstateen0 bit 58 is performed before this indirect register access.

imsic_csr_write() writes CSR_SISELECT then CSR_SIREG to program IMSIC EIP[k]/EIE[k] registers. Same vulnerability: no check of mstateen0[58] or sstateen0[58] before the indirect CSR access. This function is called from imsic_local_delivery(), __imsic_eix_update(), and the local sync path — all operate without the state-enable guard.

KVM imsic_vs_csr_read() macro accesses guest IMSIC registers via CSR_VSISELECT/CSR_VSIREG. KVM correctly configures hstateen0 with SMSTATEEN0_AIA_IMSIC for the guest, but if mstateen0[58] is 0, writing hstateen0[58]=1 has no architectural effect — the host's own siselect/sireg accesses would fault. This silently breaks KVM IMSIC virtualization when M-mode firmware does not set the bit.

KVM correctly sets hstateen0 with SMSTATEEN0_AIA_IMSIC | SMSTATEEN0_AIA | SMSTATEEN0_AIA_ISEL when the guest ISA includes SSAIA. This is the correct virtualization behavior: KVM's job is to configure hstateen0 to grant the guest access to these CSRs. The underlying issue (mstateen0[58] being zero) is M-mode firmware's responsibility, not KVM's. KVM cannot fix a broken M-mode firmware configuration from HS-mode.

The Smstateen bit definitions are correctly defined: SMSTATEEN0_AIA_IMSIC at bit 58, SMSTATEEN0_AIA at bit 59, SMSTATEEN0_AIA_ISEL at bit 60. CSR addresses STOPEI (0x15c), SISELECT (0x150), SIREG (0x151) are correctly defined. The infrastructure for checking these bits exists but is never used by the S-mode IMSIC driver at runtime.
findings.snippet:
#define SMSTATEEN0_AIA_IMSIC_SHIFT   58
#define SMSTATEEN0_AIA_IMSIC          (_ULL(1) << SMSTATEEN0_AIA_IMSIC_SHIFT)
#define SMSTATEEN0_AIA_SHIFT         59
#define SMSTATEEN0_AIA                (_ULL(1) << SMSTATEEN0_AIA_SHIFT)
#define SMSTATEEN0_AIA_ISEL_SHIFT    60

findings.finding: imsic_vsfile_local_read() accesses IMSIC VS-file registers (EIDELIVERY, EITHRESHOLD, EIP[k], EIE[k]) via CSR_VSISELECT/CSR_VSIREG on a remote CPU using on_each_cpu_mask(). If mstateen0[58] is zero, this IPI-based cross-CPU access will trap with an illegal-instruction exception on the target CPU's S-mode context, potentially crashing that CPU or triggering undefined behavior in the IPI handler.

hgei_interrupt() only reads CSR_HGEIP and CSR_HGEIE and writes CSR_HGEIE — these are hypervisor-level CSRs not gated by mstateen0 bit 58. The IMSIC-specific CSRs (stopei/eip/eie) gated by bit 58 are accessed in the aia_imsic.c functions called later in the VCPU run loop, not in this interrupt handler itself.
